latin: Licet dei uoluntas consequens semper impleatur, non tamen necessitatem rebus uolitis generaliter imponit.
translation: Although God's consequent will is always fulfilled, it does not, however, impose necessity on willed things in general.
translation_note: 'uoluntas consequens' (consequent will) is the scholastic term for God's will as it bears on things all considered together, contrasted with his antecedent will toward each thing considered in itself, per Edelheit's citation of the parallel Thomistic text (edelheit2022:10386).
translator: original translation, drafted 2026-09-26 by WRITER-full-batch2, from Latin at farmer1998:11328

sources.text: Thomas Aquinas, Summa theologiae, 1, question 23, article 5
sources.pico_relation: Edelheit continues his discussion of thesis 2.6 into this thesis, from the same article on predestination

doctrine: The thesis holds that although God's consequent will is always fulfilled, it does not thereby impose necessity on willed things in general (farmer1998:11328). Edelheit reports that in thesis 7 the will of God will always be fulfilled, yet it does not impose in a general fashion necessity upon things willed (res volitae), and continues his discussion from thesis 6's citation of Thomas's Summa theologiae, 1, question 23, article 5 (edelheit2022:10386). Farmer groups this thesis with 2.2-9 under the divine omnipotence/free will problem (farmer1998:11348).
historiography: Edelheit (2022) quotes Pico's Latin at page 220 of the 900 Theses alongside Thomas's statement, from the same article, that predestination is ordered to the divine goodness as its end (edelheit2022:10409).

quotations.text: In thesis 7 we find that, although the will of God will always be fulfilled, yet it does not impose in a general fashion necessity upon things willed (res volitae).

not_established: Not established by the sources consulted.
